title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: something lives in the earth, and the earth doesn't know it. how?

segments.voice: Last week, tat tvam asi climbed its stairs: the finest essence, the real, the self, and a son who kept asking for more. Today, one school's way of reading the line.
screen: `ASKING AGAIN IS HOW IT GOES ON.`

segments.voice: An airport gate. Someone in line turns around, and the face takes a second. A teacher from third grade? Grayer now, different glasses, a different city, years later. Then it clicks, and the sentence comes out by itself: that's her. Nobody hearing it is confused. Advaita teachers reach for exactly this kind of sentence to explain tat tvam asi. But how can then-her and now-her be one person?
screen: `A FACE AT THE GATE.` → `GRAYER, YEARS LATER.` → `THAT'S HER.` → `HOW IS IT THE SAME PERSON?`

segments.voice: The example comes from a teaching manual called the Vedantasara, not from the Chandogya itself. Its sentence is: this is that Devadatta. Devadatta is a stock name in old Sanskrit examples, a bit like John Doe. Here's the logic, in paraphrase. That Devadatta means the man as he was, then, there. This Devadatta means the man as he is, now, here. Then and now can't both be true of him at once. So you quietly set aside the time and the place, and keep the person. Now try it on tat tvam asi. In the Advaita reading, that points to awareness in the language of the vast and the far: knowing everything, beyond sight. You points to awareness in the language of the small and the near: this body, this mind, this one life. As labels, they clash. So both sets of labels are set aside, and what's left is the one awareness both words pointed at. Notice what this reading doesn't say. It doesn't say your ego is God. The little labels of you go just as firmly as the grand labels of that. What remains isn't a bigger me. In this school's reading, it's awareness without the labels. Other schools hear the line differently, and the next two days give them their turn.
screen: `THIS IS THAT DEVADATTA.` · `SET ASIDE THEN AND NOW.` · `SET ASIDE THE LABELS, BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `NOT A BIGGER ME.`

segments.voice: Write your name on a scrap of paper, and under it two or three labels you carry: a role, a job, a nickname. Read each one, then set the pen down and let the labels stay there on the page. Rest a while in the plain awareness that read them.
Tat tvam asi, read the Advaita way: set the labels aside on both sides, and one awareness is left.
Keep this one: tat tvam asi, this is that Devadatta, older now and the very same. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1758 COUNTS.` → `TAT TVAM ASI · 7 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE EARTH, AND UNKNOWN TO IT?`

howItsDone: In Advaita study, students learn the Vedantasara's 'this is that Devadatta' as a standard way of explaining how tat tvam asi points past the labels of both words.

notes: Block 'tat tvam asi', day 7 of 9 (1752–1760); first day of the week 1758–1764, so the review says 'last week'.

The airport scene is the lesson's own framing; the sentence 'this is that Devadatta' (so 'yam devadattah) is the Vedantasara's example. Confirm the section and that it is the Vedantasara (not only the Vakyavritti) that gives it.

'Awareness in the language of the vast and the far: knowing everything, beyond sight' summarizes the Vedantasara's qualifiers of 'that' (remoteness, omniscience); 'the small and the near' summarizes those of 'you' (immediacy, limited knowing). Confirm.

The trapdoor's 'partial setting-aside' renders bhaga-tyaga (jahad-ajahal) lakshana. Confirm the term the Vedantasara uses. The lesson calls Devadatta 'a stock name, a bit like John Doe'; no etymology is given on purpose.
